title: REVELATION CALLS BABYLON A PROSTITUTE: What Is the Sexual Imagery Really About?
paragraphs:
REVELATION CALLS BABYLON A PROSTITUTE: What Is the Sexual Imagery Really About?
The woman in Revelation 17 is seductive, wealthy, powerful, and drunk with blood. But if you think this chapter is mainly about sex, you may have missed the terrifying warning John was actually giving the Church.
There are passages in the Bible we read quietly.
And then there are passages that seem to grab us by the shoulders.
She is dressed in purple and scarlet. Gold flashes from her body. Precious stones and pearls announce wealth, status, beauty, influence.
There is a golden cup in her hand.
Everything about her says, Come closer.
Then John tells us what is inside the cup.
And suddenly the beauty becomes horrifying.
Because Revelation is showing us something every generation desperately needs to understand:
Evil does not always approach you looking evil.
Sometimes rebellion against God is profitable.
Sometimes the thing destroying your soul is holding a golden cup.
And sometimes Babylon does not ask you to deny Jesus.
She simply offers you enough other things to love that eventually Jesus no longer has first place.
That is where this becomes personal.
Revelation 17 opens with language so graphic that modern readers sometimes become fixated on the sexual imagery itself. John writes of:
τῆς πόρνης τῆς μεγάλης — tēs pornēs tēs megalēs

The Greek noun πόρνη — pornē refers to a prostitute. Revelation then uses the related language of πορνεύω — porneuō, “to commit sexual immorality/prostitution,” and πορνεία — porneia, sexual immorality or prostitution.
John is not sanitizing his vocabulary.
He wants the image to disturb us.
But here is where careful Bible reading matters.
The sexual imagery is not permission to reduce Revelation 17 to a chapter about literal sexual immorality.
John eventually interprets his own symbol.
The woman is identified as ἡ πόλις ἡ μεγάλη — hē polis hē megalē:
She represents a civilization, a system of power, wealth, seduction, idolatry, oppression, luxury, political influence, economic intoxication, and hostility toward those who belong to Jesus.

For John’s first hearers, the imagery would naturally evoke the imperial world surrounding them, and the seven mountains of Revelation 17:9 have historically made the connection with Rome especially significant. Yet John deliberately calls her not simply Rome, but Babylon.
Because Babylon was already larger than one city in the biblical imagination.
Babylon represented humanity organized in proud resistance against God.
We can define good and evil without Him.
We can become glorious without Him.
We can have the gifts of creation while rejecting the Creator.

The prophets had already used sexual unfaithfulness as a devastating picture of covenant betrayal and idolatry. God was not trivializing sexuality. He was drawing upon one of humanity’s deepest relational realities—faithfulness between those who belong to one another—to expose what idolatry actually means.
Idolatry is not merely choosing the wrong religious object.
It is giving another lover what belongs to God.
That is why Revelation’s imagery cuts so deeply.
Babylon does not merely want your money.
She does not merely want participation.
She does not simply sell products.
She sells a vision of life where God becomes unnecessary.
And suddenly Revelation 17 is no longer about some strange woman at the end of history.
Suddenly she is standing much closer.
Because Babylon whispers every time something created says:
“I can give you what only God can give you.”
Religious prestige can even become Babylon.
Anything becomes spiritually adulterous when we demand from it the identity, security, satisfaction, glory, or salvation that belongs to God alone.
And here is the frightening part.
John does not see a miserable woman dressed in rags.
Because Satan rarely needs to make destruction ugly when he can make it desirable.
Some temptations would be easy to resist if they looked like death.
So they arrive looking like life.
That relationship you know requires disobedience.
That private habit nobody knows about.
That willingness to compromise because the money is good.
That resentment you secretly enjoy rehearsing.
That version of Christianity where Jesus is Savior but never Lord.
That carefully maintained public image hiding a starving private soul.
That does not mean what is inside it is holy.
And maybe that is why Revelation makes us uncomfortable.
We would rather identify Babylon “out there.”
But Revelation was given to churches.
Christians were expected to hear this warning.
Because the question is not merely:
“What part of Babylon is still living in me?”
What can you not imagine losing?
What secret pleasure repeatedly defeats your devotion?
What do you reach for when your soul hurts before you reach for Christ?
What would devastate you more—losing your reputation or grieving the Holy Spirit?
Because idols rarely introduce themselves as idols.
And slowly the golden cup reaches your lips.
Revelation says the nations become intoxicated.
Something can be obviously destructive to a sober person and seem completely reasonable to someone intoxicated.
Repeated compromise does not merely break commandments.
Eventually we can call bondage freedom.
The woman is not merely seductive.
John sees her drunk with “the blood of the saints” and with the blood of those who bear witness to Jesus.
The Greek word connected with witness here is μάρτυς — martys.
It is the word from which English eventually receives “martyr.”
Babylon persecutes those she cannot seduce.
Revelation 17:14 gives away the ending before Babylon even falls:
Because He is Lord of lords and King of kings.
There is the center of the chapter.
This is something we repeatedly get wrong when reading Revelation.
We become fascinated with the beast and forget the Lamb.
We chase timelines and overlook worship.
We argue over symbols while ignoring repentance.
We attempt to identify Babylon while Babylon's values quietly colonize our hearts.
But Revelation was not written merely to satisfy curiosity about tomorrow.
It was written to produce faithfulness today.
And that means the appropriate response to Revelation 17 is not:
“Who can I accuse of being Babylon?”
“Jesus, show me where I have been drinking from her cup.”
Maybe your Christianity has become a performance.
Maybe you know worship songs but barely know the One being worshiped.
Maybe your Bible gathers dust while your screen receives hours of your attention.
Maybe pornography has been discipling your imagination.
Maybe money has been discipling your decisions.
Maybe outrage has been discipling your emotions.
Maybe approval has been discipling your identity.
Maybe comfort has been discipling your obedience.
Maybe you have learned how to appear spiritually alive while privately becoming numb.
You remember when conviction came quickly.
You remember when prayer felt less complicated.
You remember when you wanted Jesus more than you wanted the appearance of wanting Jesus.
And perhaps reading this has uncovered the thing you have been trying not to name.
Jesus exposes what He intends to heal.
The Gospel is not the announcement that clean people are welcomed while dirty people are rejected.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners can come home because Jesus Christ took judgment upon Himself.
That is why the imagery of Revelation must never become an excuse for Christians to shame sexually broken people.
Jesus was repeatedly compassionate toward people carrying sexual shame while remaining absolutely truthful about sin.
Remember the woman caught in adultery.
Remember the Samaritan woman whose relational history Jesus already knew.
Christ did not need their secrets explained to Him.
Still He called people away from sin.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus does not save us because our history is respectable.
He saves us because His blood is sufficient.
You may have committed sexual sin.
You may have lived for money.
You may have sold pieces of your conscience for acceptance.
You may have consumed things privately you would be horrified for anyone to discover.
You may have spent years drinking from Babylon's cup.
But Babylon does not get the final word over your identity.
The cross means your worst chapter does not have authority to write your ending.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you out of the burning building.
That is why another voice eventually thunders in Revelation:
God is calling His people away from participation in Babylon.
Not because Babylon has nothing attractive to offer.
Come out precisely because it does.
Come out before luxury becomes your master.
Come out before compromise becomes normal.
Come out before your conscience stops hurting.
Come out before you exchange eternal treasure for temporary applause.
Come out before the golden cup convinces you that poison is wine.
That is the unavoidable message of Revelation 18.
The economic machine that seemed untouchable collapses.
And heaven does not mourn Babylon as though God's kingdom has suffered defeat.
That is the choice Revelation places before us.
Babylon says, “Buy enough and you will matter.”
Jesus says you were worth His blood before you could purchase anything.
Babylon holds a golden cup filled with corruption.
Jesus took another cup—the cup of suffering—and drank what sinners deserved.
Revelation is ultimately presenting competing loves.
Christ gives Himself for His bride.
And when Babylon's beauty has turned to ashes...
Maybe you needed that sentence tonight.
Maybe everything you trusted has been shaking.
Maybe something you thought would satisfy you has left you emptier.
Maybe sin promised pleasure and handed you chains.
Maybe success gave you applause but stole your peace.
Maybe religion gave you an image while your heart remained far from God.
Not after you erase your history.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is no scandal so filthy that His grace becomes insufficient for the genuinely repentant sinner.
There is no chain so respectable that Jesus will allow us to keep calling it freedom.
Grace does not merely forgive the old life.
Grace begins transforming us into something new.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior keeps returning to the same heartbeat:
You do not need impressive words.
Sometimes surrender begins with four words spoken honestly.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
But sometimes publicly admitting that we need mercy is one small way of refusing to hide anymore.
Someone reading may desperately need proof that chains really can break.
Not merely because an algorithm rewards sharing.
They may sit beside you in church.
And they may be silently wondering whether Jesus would still receive them if anyone knew the truth.
Send it privately to someone who needs grace more than another lecture.
There is also a practical reality behind this ministry.
Biblical content, discipleship resources, books, research, outreach, and the continued building of resources for believers require people willing to stand behind the work.
It does not make someone a better Christian.
It does not earn spiritual blessing.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can help that work continue reaching people with Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and the hope found in Jesus Christ.
“Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved.”
Our mission is simply to keep pointing people toward Him.
The houses belong to somebody else.
And every glittering thing this world told us we could not live without will finally reveal how temporary it always was.
But Jesus Christ will still be King.
So before you take another drink from the cup this world keeps passing around...
And choose carefully what gets your heart.
Because the most dangerous thing about Babylon was never that she looked evil—it was that she looked beautiful enough to make people forget they were made for God.
